classification.difficultyReason: Complete supplied distance definitions, sign-based cases and elementary identities; the main decision is to test the sign of f(x) when defining |f(x)|.

questions.mappingNote: Use the sign of the absolute-value argument to complete the cases; interpret absolute value as distance for the remaining parts.
questions.methodNote: Separate teaching evidence was not supplied. The question supplies distance definitions, two-case scaffolds and elementary identities.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall that absolute-value outputs are non-negative and identify the vocabulary for sharp graph points; no calculation or linked procedure is required.

questions.mappingNote: These completions assess non-negative outputs and graph vocabulary; retain the source term cusps.
questions.methodNote: Separate teaching evidence was not supplied. Use the distance interpretation and characteristic sharp point of the absolute-value graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete standard symmetry, product and quotient identities and recall that the denominator must be nonzero; each part is a direct application.

questions.mappingNote: Use distance symmetry for parts a–b and magnitude rules for parts c–d, retaining the nonzero denominator condition.
questions.methodNote: Separate teaching evidence was not supplied. The question requests standard absolute-value symmetry, product and quotient identities.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly interpret absolute value as distance, first from zero and then from the specified centre b; no equation solving is required.

questions.mappingNote: Interpret the first expression as distance from zero and the translated expression as distance from b. Keep both answer diagrams in solution content.
questions.methodNote: Separate teaching evidence was not supplied. The question explicitly requests the number-line distance interpretation; the inspected answer key illustrates it with paired curved distance arrows.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate numerical absolute values directly, including one subtraction before taking the nonnegative magnitude.

questions.mappingNote: Each of the three numerical expressions directly assesses the absolute-value definition.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate absolute value as distance from the origin; the question itself supplies the task.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the supplied signed values into both sides of each identity, evaluate products, quotients and differences, and compare the numerical results.

questions.mappingNote: All four identities require numerical verification, rather than a general proof.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the supplied values into each side and evaluate separately.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete explicit distance-method steps by identifying centres and distances, finding two positions, normalising a coefficient as prompted, and reversing the sign of an absolute-value argument.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c identify centre and distance; d normalises first; e retains the sign-reversal response without adding an extra solving task.
questions.methodNote: The printed completion scaffolds explicitly teach distance from a centre, coefficient normalisation and sign reversal.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate absolute-value equations into symmetric number-line diagrams, normalising coefficients and reversing the argument's sign where needed; the preceding scaffold and supplied diagram model the representation.

questions.mappingNote: Four unlettered response leaves retain the implicit tasks for Question 3(b)–(e). Equations are repeated so the selectable question carries its own givens.
questions.methodNote: The permanent supplied diagram models equal distances on either side of a centre; Question 3 supplies normalisation and sign reversal.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the specified distance method: normalise a linear argument, identify its centre and radius, and calculate both endpoints, including a sign-reversed argument.

questions.mappingNote: All eight equations have their own givens. Worked answers retain the explicitly requested distance method.
questions.methodNote: Use Question 3's distance method: normalise the coefficient, identify centre and distance, then move that distance in both directions.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete supplied positive-and-negative-case statements and recognise invariance under negating the absolute-value argument; the scaffold supplies the equation structure and does not require solving the resulting linear equations.

questions.mappingNote: The response is the missing number or expression, rather than an added request to finish solving.
questions.methodNote: The supplied scaffolds introduce the positive and negative cases and sign reversal.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught positive and negative cases, then solve routine linear equations; the fractional arguments require clearing a constant denominator, without an additional conceptual decision.

questions.mappingNote: All nine equations directly assess algebraic absolute-value solving; h and i retain stacked fractions.
questions.methodNote: Use the positive and negative algebraic cases introduced in Question 6, with sign reversal where useful.

classification.difficultyReason: Test f(-x) against f(x) and -f(x), using absolute-value identities; part (c) additionally requires finding the denominator restriction and recognising that an asymmetric domain rules out both parity classifications.

questions.mappingNote: All four source parts assess parity; part (c) requires attention to the domain.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Use the even/odd tests and check domain symmetry.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish valid absolute-value identities from sign-dependent claims and choose a specific counterexample for each false claim, including recognising that the principal square root is non-negative.

questions.mappingNote: The six identities include the directly assessed square-root identity in part (f).
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Evaluate a specific counterexample for each false statement; use absolute-value properties for true statements.

classification.difficultyReason: Locate each zero of the absolute-value argument and sketch two upward branches with gradients -1 and 1; recognise that |3-x|=|x-3| when positioning the final vertex.

questions.mappingNote: Four independent translated absolute-value graph tasks; source prints four columns without supplied axes.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Branch equations locate each vertex and determine the V-shaped sketch.

classification.difficultyReason: Find each linear argument's zero, identify the left and right gradients, and sketch the resulting V; the requested vertex and gradients explicitly guide the graph construction.

questions.mappingNote: Each part has a zero of the linear argument, two branch gradients and a graph.
questions.methodNote: The printed instruction explicitly requires finding vertices and branch gradients before sketching; separate teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied definition to split each linear argument at zero, negate the negative branch and state the corresponding domains; solving 2x-3≥0 is routine.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded definition is permanent parent content and directly governs each of the three branch/domain responses.
questions.methodNote: The inspected question supplies the piecewise definition. Split according to whether the linear argument is non-negative or negative.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify the quotient separately for positive and negative x, recognise that zero is excluded, and connect the supplied branch scaffold and completed table to horizontal rays with open endpoints.

questions.mappingNote: Keep all four dependent parts together; the quotient is undefined at zero throughout.
questions.methodNote: The inspected question sequences a branch boundary, piecewise completion, value table and graph. The embedded definition in Question 12 supplies the absolute-value rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Split at x=0, simplify each expression on both domains, and translate the resulting linear or quadratic branches into a joined sketch using the preceding method.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts require both domain-dependent formulas and sketches. Teacher page 28 confirms these results but is answer evidence, not a teaching page.
questions.methodNote: Split the absolute value at x=0, simplify each branch, then sketch. The referenced student Question 13 was not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct two graphs on common axes, identify the absolute-value branches, and interpret their intersections as equation solutions; the parts explicitly guide each representation change.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) share the student-drawn axes and one labelled answer figure. Parts (c) and (d) use the same intersections.
questions.methodNote: The question itself scaffolds solving an equation geometrically: sketch both graphs, label the absolute value branches, interpret intersections, then read the solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose and sketch comparison graphs for each equation, then interpret two, zero or one intersections; the no-solution case requires recognising the sign restriction and parallel nonnegative branches without intermediate prompts.

questions.mappingNote: Each part supplies its own complete equation. The reference to Question 15 identifies a method rather than missing mathematical givens.
questions.methodNote: Use the graphical intersection procedure explicitly scaffolded by Question 15 on the inspected source page.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover each horizontal shift from the vertex, determine the scale from a labelled point, and express the result as |ax+b|; the final part requires using a fractional vertex.

questions.mappingNote: Each source graph remains a question diagram in its original two-column reading order. Answers use a positive scale factor, giving the key's equivalent absolute value expressions.
questions.methodNote: Recover each equation from its vertex and one labelled point. No separate source teaching page was supplied to verify the original worked method.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine restricted absolute-value and quadratic branches, then solve each requested output on both domains and reject candidates outside their branch conditions.

questions.mappingNote: The complete piecewise rule is a permanent given in the parent prompt. Each requested sketch or input set has a separate answer-owning child. No separate teaching page was supplied.
questions.methodNote: Apply each formula only on its stated domain. Sketch the branches and solve for a specified output separately on each domain, rejecting inputs outside that domain.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the requested piecewise representation to split |x| at zero, then sketch the appropriate restricted quadratic branches and join them at the origin.

questions.mappingNote: The stem explicitly requires the piecewise method. No teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Split |x| at zero and sketch the resulting restricted quadratics.

classification.difficultyReason: Factor the numerator, distinguish the two signs of x-1 in the absolute-value denominator, preserve the excluded input after cancellation, and sketch two restricted lines with distinct open endpoints.

questions.mappingNote: The expression and 'hence' connect simplification to sketching. No teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Factor the numerator, split by the sign of x-1, preserve the original domain, and sketch restricted lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that absolute value is nonnegative while −1−x² is strictly negative, and explain why these sign ranges exclude equality without solving.

questions.mappingNote: This reasoning is explicitly requested by the source question; no teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Compare signs without solving.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete explicitly scaffolded signed cases, solve the remaining linear equation, and validate its fractional candidate by substitution and the supplied nonnegative-output restriction.

questions.mappingNote: The complete supplied demonstration and both checking routes are embedded in Problem 4 and remain permanently visible.
questions.methodNote: Form two linear cases and validate candidates either by substitution or by the nonnegative-output condition.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct two absolute-value graphs with different vertices and branch gradients on common axes, locate both intersections, and interpret their x-coordinates as equation solutions.

questions.mappingNote: The source explicitly requires a geometric method. The answer key gives only values; no teaching pages establish a preferred geometric construction.
questions.methodNote: Solve geometrically using intersections of the two absolute-value graphs.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain when signed linear cases require a nonnegative-right-side check, distinguish a variable right side from a positive constant, and justify why equality of two absolute values introduces no sign-invalid candidates.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied scaffold in Problem 4 on this page establishes checking candidates. Each part of Problem 6 retains its own equations.
questions.methodNote: Distinguish candidate generation from validity checking using nonnegative absolute-value outputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish a conditional implication from an unrestricted equation-solving rule, recognise that its premise already forces k≥0, and justify both sign cases rather than treating negative k as a counterexample.

questions.mappingNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The literal implication is preserved; it differs from the unrestricted solution rule apparently intended by the key.
questions.methodNote: Apply the piecewise definition to assess the printed implication.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate equal coordinate magnitudes into y=x or y=−x and combine both complete lines in one relation sketch, rather than drawing only the familiar absolute-value V.

questions.mappingNote: The source requests a relation sketch. The matched key confirms both complete lines; separate teaching pages were not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Equal absolute values give two possible signed coordinate relationships.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer x≥0 from the nonnegative absolute value, derive y=±x, and apply the restriction to sketch two right-opening rays with their common endpoint included.

questions.mappingNote: Problem 9 directly assesses sketching a relation with absolute value applied to y. No teaching pages were supplied; the method is independently derived and agrees with the inspected P9 answer graph.
questions.methodNote: Use the nonnegative output of absolute value to restrict x, then sketch the two branches y=x and y=-x for x>=0.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the inverse-proportion formula and constant terminology, and identify reciprocal change with the positive-branch conditions and sentence scaffolds supplied.

questions.mappingNote: Part a identifies the denominator; b and c describe reciprocal change on the positive branch; d names the constant.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The embedded definition y=k/x supports the reciprocal and constant-product reasoning.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply standard properties of y=k/x to identify axis asymptotes, excluded domain and range values, and quadrants from the sign of k.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b assess coordinate-axis asymptotes; c–d assess domain and range; e–f assess quadrants from the sign of k.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Use the reciprocal relationship, its excluded zero denominator, and the signs of x and y.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate each reciprocal equation into a two-branch sketch using its sign and axis asymptotes, then choose and evaluate a convenient nonzero x-value to label a point.

questions.mappingNote: All four equations assess unshifted reciprocal sketches. Part d retains 2x as the complete denominator.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The nearby Fundamentals questions establish the quadrants and coordinate-axis asymptotes. Substitute a convenient x-value to label a point.

classification.difficultyReason: Read a marked point from each supplied reciprocal graph, calculate k=xy and identify the two coordinate-axis asymptotes; both parts directly apply the taught graph model.

questions.mappingNote: The left graph supplies (3,1), giving k=3. The right graph supplies (-2,2), giving k=-4. Both retain their supplied graph as visible question evidence.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Read the guided point and use the embedded reciprocal definition to obtain k=xy; identify the axes approached by the branches.

classification.difficultyReason: Form the reciprocal model, determine its constant, evaluate a new value and translate the model into a two-branch sketch showing both data points; the parts scaffold these routine linked representations.

questions.mappingNote: The model, constant, substitution and requested hyperbola directly support the selected skills. No separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: The supplied question establishes inverse proportionality. Use xy=k, determine k from the given pair, substitute the new x-value, then sketch y=6/x.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the inverse pair while distance is fixed, calculate the journey constant and use the explicitly supplied relationship to find time and speed; the formula and staged prompts make the applications direct.

questions.mappingNote: All five parts concern speed and time for the same fixed journey. Both supplied formulas remain visible in their original owning prompts. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: The question supplies D=ST and T=k/S. Hold distance fixed, find k=ST, then substitute or rearrange the reciprocal model.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the stated inverse pressure-volume relationship into PV=k, determine the shared constant and rearrange for either variable under changed conditions; these are routine linked modelling steps.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts use the same initial pressure and volume. The embedded law remains in the shared prompt. No separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: The shared stem explicitly gives inverse proportionality. Find the constant PV, then divide it by the new pressure or volume, retaining exact fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a doubled input into the supplied inverse model and recognise k/x₁ as y₁ to establish the requested identity; apply the same relationship to halving and tripling.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) requires a symbolic demonstration; the remaining parts state its multiplicative consequences. The two subparts of (c) retain the source's two-column row. Separate teaching pages were unavailable.
questions.methodNote: The question supplies y=k/x and initial notation x_1,y_1. Substitute the scaled x-value and express the new value in terms of y_1.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain the fixed-work inverse relationship, define variables and determine the constant product, then use the resulting model to calculate either time or workforce.

questions.mappingNote: The explanation and model apply to the same fixed job and given workforce and duration. The constant-rate assumption makes the explanation mathematically sufficient. No separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Part (b) explicitly assumes inverse variation. Define the variables, find the invariant product PD, and use P=300/D or D=300/P.

classification.difficultyReason: Use a positive-parameter slider to interpret changes in a hyperbola, locate the specified intersection with y=x, and translate that graphical result into a substitution verifying k=16.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is describing parameter effects on y=k/x; the final part verifies the graphical result by substitution.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The question itself prescribes graphing software and a positive-parameter slider, followed by algebraic verification.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the two soldier counts, use the constant soldier-days product to find the new duration, and subtract it from 20 days to answer how much less time the food lasts.

questions.mappingNote: The question asks for the reduction in duration, requiring both the inverse-variation calculation and subtraction from 20 days.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The source explicitly assumes inverse variation, so the solution uses a constant product.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive a constant-product identity from inverse variation, use it to deduce a ratio relationship, then assign the soldier and duration values and interpret the reduction in days. The labelled steps and supplied target identity scaffold these linked procedures.

questions.mappingNote: The solution follows the printed derivation and applies the derived ratio directly, without calculating a constant of proportionality in part (c).
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Parts (a) and (b) explicitly scaffold derivation of the constant-product and inverse-ratio identities; part (c) requires the ratio method.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the origin-centred and translated circle equations from the stated centre and radius; no linked calculation is required.

questions.mappingNote: The general circle-equation skill directly covers part (b); the origin-centred skill covers part (a).
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The two statements assess recall of the origin-centred and translated circle equations.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the centre and radius from the square-root form and connect the sign of each branch to the upper or lower semicircle, with the reasoning scaffold supplied.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts identify origin-centred semicircles and interpret their vertical coordinates.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The question itself explains the sign of the square-root branches.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute each centre and radius into the circle equation, handling negative centre coordinates and squaring numerical or symbolic radii.

questions.mappingNote: Substitute the specified centre and radius into the general circle equation; part (a) uses its origin-centred form.
questions.methodNote: Fundamentals 1 on the assigned practice page supplies the equation-recall context; separate teaching evidence is unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Place each centre on coordinate axes and use its radius to sketch the circle with the correct axis relationships, including tangency and a circle wholly within quadrant II.

questions.mappingNote: The four parts reproduce the givens from Question 1(a)-(d), making the selectable question self-contained while retaining its dependency.
questions.methodNote: Separate graphing instruction was not supplied. Centre-and-radius sketches are supported by the task and its four keyed figures.

classification.difficultyReason: Find each coordinate interval directly by subtracting and adding the supplied radius to the corresponding centre coordinate, retaining exact surd and fractional bounds.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses domain and range. The givens from Question 1(a)-(d) are repeated to make this selectable question self-contained.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence is unavailable. Use the horizontal and vertical extremes, obtained by adding and subtracting the radius from the corresponding centre coordinate.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the square in the coordinate terms, read the centre and radius from standard form, then use those parameters to obtain domain and range.

questions.mappingNote: Complete the square in each coordinate, compare with the general circle equation, then use centre coordinate plus or minus radius for the bounds.
questions.methodNote: The printed instruction explicitly requires completing the square. Separate teaching examples are unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret intercepts, tangencies and centre guides to identify each circle, then construct its equation; part (d) requires using the distance from (1,1) to the origin to obtain the radius.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a)–(d) directly assess circle equations with translated centres. Method fidelity to the textbook's teaching pages remains unverified.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Read the centre and radius from the graph, then substitute into (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2; use the distance from (1,1) to the origin in part (d).

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the radius from each radicand, use the sign of the square root to choose the upper or lower half, and plot the intercepts; all four parts directly apply the semicircle form.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess graphing semicircles from square-root equations; the inspected answer graphs confirm orientation and intercepts.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Identify r from r^2, choose the upper or lower half using the sign of the square root, and plot the three intercept points.

classification.difficultyReason: Read each labelled radius, square it inside the radical and select the root sign from the graph's orientation; no inference beyond the standard semicircle form is required.

questions.mappingNote: Each diagram directly assesses a semicircle equation. The answer evidence confirms all four radii and signs.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Read the radius, square it inside the radical, and select the positive or negative square root from the semicircle's orientation.

classification.difficultyReason: After plotting the endpoints, use the supplied hint to find their midpoint, calculate the squared radius from an endpoint and substitute into the translated-circle equation. This links routine coordinate procedures with explicit support.

questions.mappingNote: Both plotted endpoints and the dependent diameter task remain in one selectable question. The most advanced directly assessed skill is the equation of a circle with a translated centre. Broader textbook teaching evidence is unavailable.
questions.methodNote: The embedded source hint explicitly requires finding the centre first. Use the midpoint of the diameter, then the squared distance to either endpoint.

classification.difficultyReason: Rewrite the radical equation as an origin-centred circle, determine its radius and intercepts, and retain only the upper branch required by the square root.

questions.mappingNote: The assigned equation directly assesses graphing a semicircle; the P1 answer diagram confirms the intercepts and branch.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. Square the equation, identify the circle, then retain the upper half required by the square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the square in two variables to locate the scanner, calculate the ships' separation, and interpret that same distance against two different detection radii.

questions.mappingNote: The expanded circle equation directly assesses the general circle equation. The nested detection questions use the same two ships and preserve their shared stem.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. Complete the square to identify the centre and radius, then compare the distance between the ships with each scanner radius.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect expanded equations with circle and hyperbola graphs, infer parameter-dependent contact points from software, and choose an algebraic elimination that verifies the conjecture; the expansion hint and staged investigation supply substantial support.

questions.mappingNote: All five parts retain the circle–hyperbola investigation within one selectable practice question. Intersection-line-curve is the closest supplied catalogue skill for the final simultaneous-equation task; the original system contains two curves.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. The question itself supplies expansion as the hint, graphing software and a parameter slider for conjecture, then simultaneous equations for verification.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall continuity terminology and construct familiar sketches of a jump, a hole and a vertical-asymptote discontinuity; the initial-letter prompts support direct application.

questions.mappingNote: All five printed F1 parts are retained as selectable practice. No separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use the informal unbroken-graph definition, the specified domain, denominator zeros and the three illustrated discontinuity types embedded in this task and its answer evidence.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify unbroken graphs, a vertical asymptote, a hole and a jump, then read the discontinuity coordinates; recognise that a joined corner is continuous.

questions.mappingNote: This graphical classification method is supported by the adjacent Fundamentals 1 task and the matching Q1 answer entries. Separate teaching pages were unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Inspect each supplied graph for an unbroken curve, a hole, a jump or a vertical asymptote; read the discontinuity's x-coordinate from the graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Match unbounded branches, unequal one-sided heights and an open point to the three supplied discontinuity categories; no calculation or additional representation is required.

questions.mappingNote: Directly assesses graphical recognition of discontinuity types.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages supplied. Independently identify unbounded behaviour, unequal one-sided values and a missing point from the graphs.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify each joining input, substitute it into the neighbouring formulas and compare their values with the defined function value, including the separately defined point in part d.

questions.mappingNote: Continuity is assessed only at the equation-change point. In part (b), the separate singularity at x=-4 is outside the requested check.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages supplied. Independently compare the neighbouring formula values at the joining point with the defined function value.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate continuity at each joining input into equality of the two formulas, then solve for the parameter; part d requires rearranging and factorising a quadratic and retaining both valid roots.

questions.mappingNote: The parameter is determined by continuity; the most advanced directly assessed skill is continuity of piecewise functions.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages supplied. Independently equate the two boundary values and solve the resulting linear or quadratic equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate branch for three inputs, evaluate each value, then combine them in the given expression using exact fraction arithmetic.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded definition is permanent question content. Selecting among three formulas directly assesses interpretation of a piecewise function.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages supplied. Independently select each formula using its interval condition, evaluate each function value, then substitute into the combined expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Match each supplied input to its branch, turn its known output into an equation, and solve three independent linear equations for the coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: The three conditions determine separate coefficients in separate branches; the definition remains visible in the prompt.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages supplied. Independently choose the formula for each supplied input, substitute the known output and solve for its coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify both branch boundaries and equate adjacent rule values at each boundary to determine two independent parameters.

questions.mappingNote: The given piecewise function assesses continuity at x=2 and x=6; the teacher key confirms both parameters.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Match the values of adjacent rules at each boundary.

classification.difficultyReason: Critique a supplied argument by recognising that the principal square root is nonnegative, identifying the extraneous candidate introduced by squaring, and connecting its failed substitution to the continuity claim.

questions.mappingNote: The intentionally incorrect argument is permanent question content. Its equations, instruction and conclusion remain visible for critique.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Check a candidate obtained by squaring in the original equation and use the nonnegative principal square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall which circular functions have sine or cosine denominators and identify the four with discontinuities; the task asks only for function names, without requiring locations or sketches.

questions.mappingNote: The source explicitly recalls the six circular functions and asks only which have discontinuities on the interval.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Identify zeros of the sine or cosine denominator in quotient and reciprocal circular functions.

classification.difficultyReason: Factor and cancel while retaining the original domain restriction, represent the excluded point as a hole, then use the preceding line sketch to supply the missing value in a continuous piecewise definition. The linked parts explicitly scaffold these connections.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts remain together. Teacher page 33 confirms the two sketches and hole; teacher page 34 supplies the continuous extension.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The question itself scaffolds the method: sketch the line, compare the rational graph after factoring, then fill its missing value.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall familiar function terminology and quadratic formulas from supplied statements, with initial letters supporting most vocabulary responses.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e respectively assess function terminology, linear-function terminology, inequalities, simultaneous equations and break-even, and quadratic-function terminology.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The question itself supplies recall statements and initial-letter scaffolds.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify which contextual variable depends on the other, then translate an explicit hourly rate and fixed fee into a linear equation.

questions.mappingNote: Part a identifies input and output in the designer context; part b combines the variable charge with the fixed setup fee.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable; use the given hourly rate and fixed fee to construct a linear model.

classification.difficultyReason: Isolate the variable using two routine inverse operations; division by a positive number preserves the inequality direction.

questions.mappingNote: The printed task directly assesses solving one strict linear inequality.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable; isolate the variable using inverse operations, dividing by a positive number.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve a routine two-step inequality, then translate the inclusive upper bound into a closed endpoint and leftward ray on a number line.

questions.mappingNote: A closed endpoint at 3 and a leftward ray express the non-strict upper bound.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Solve algebraically, then represent the inclusive endpoint and direction on a number line, as required by the prompt and answer figure.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct two straight-line graphs from their equations and identify the intersection as the simultaneous solution.

questions.mappingNote: The answer figure confirms an increasing line, a decreasing line and the common point (1,5).
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. The explicit graphical requirement is honoured by plotting each line and reading their intersection; substitution checks the coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange the equation with unit coefficients, substitute into the other equation, then back-substitute to obtain both unknowns.

questions.mappingNote: The coefficient 1 in x−y=1 permits x=y+1, followed by substitution and exact fractional results.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. The question specifies algebra without choosing substitution or elimination; substitution is used.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert the two zeros into linear factors, use monicity to fix the leading coefficient, and expand.

questions.mappingNote: Both zeros are retained. The negative quadratic in the key is excluded because its leading coefficient is −1.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Construct factors from the two zeros and use the printed monic condition to fix the leading coefficient at 1.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the roots from the sketch, form a quadratic with an unknown multiplier, determine it from another labelled point, and expand to general form.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied sketch directly supports this method; its correspondence with the textbook's taught sequence cannot be verified.
questions.methodNote: Use the two zeros to form a factorised quadratic, substitute the y-intercept, then expand to general form. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Read roots from the factors, calculate the y-intercept, use symmetry to locate the vertex, and combine these features into a downward-opening sketch.

questions.mappingNote: The factors and the independently matched answer sketch support the selected graph features.
questions.methodNote: Find intercepts, use symmetry to locate the vertex, and sketch a downward-opening parabola. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a stated fixed fee and per-kilometre rate directly into a linear cost model and justify its contextual assumptions.

questions.mappingNote: The initial fee and per-kilometre charge determine the intercept and gradient directly.
questions.methodNote: Model total cost as fixed charge plus rate times distance. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Define two unit prices, translate two purchases into simultaneous equations, and choose an elimination or substitution procedure to obtain the drink price.

questions.mappingNote: Each purchase supplies one equation for the same two unit prices.
questions.methodNote: Form two linear equations and solve by elimination. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect the total ticket count with the total cost, solve the resulting linear constraints, and interpret the solutions as whole-number ticket counts.

questions.mappingNote: The six-ticket total and total expenditure independently constrain the two counts.
questions.methodNote: Form count and cost equations, substitute, and check whole-number counts. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise break-even as equality of the supplied linear models, solve the resulting equation, and evaluate their common output.

questions.mappingNote: Both linear models are supplied explicitly; their intersection is the requested break-even point.
questions.methodNote: Equate cost and revenue, solve for the input, and evaluate the common output. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Form a quadratic area model from two variable side lengths, restrict it to positive dimensions, and use its graph to interpret the maximum area.

questions.mappingNote: The graph remains part of the solution; a vertex formula is not substituted for the requested graphical method.
questions.methodNote: Form the area function from the side lengths and read its maximum from a graph, as explicitly requested. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the vertex of a supplied downward-opening quadratic as the maximum, calculate its time, and substitute to obtain the height.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses the maximum of the given model; the teacher answer confirms metres as the height unit.
questions.methodNote: Locate the vertex of the downward-opening height quadratic and evaluate its height. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate capacity and strict profit requirements into simultaneous inequalities, account for whole-item quantities, and describe feasible production without assuming that all 70 items must be made.

questions.mappingNote: The production and profit conditions directly assess modelling with linear relationships.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. Translate each upper-limit or strict-profit condition into an inequality.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate two resource limits into inequalities, find their boundary intersection, identify the common first-quadrant region, and test a production plan against both limits.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) assesses feasible-region modelling; part (b) assesses interpreting the same resource constraints.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. Form resource inequalities, draw their boundary lines and identify the common first-quadrant region; test a proposed point by substitution.

classification.difficultyReason: Form profit by subtracting cost from revenue, recognise that the downward-opening quadratic is maximised at its vertex, and evaluate the profit there.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses forming and maximising a quadratic profit model.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. Form profit as revenue minus cost and use the vertex of the downward-opening quadratic. Answer page 34, Exercise 4E F1(e), explicitly lists the vertex formula x=-b/(2a), supporting this method.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall direct and inverse variation models, recognise their doubling effects, and complete method and context vocabulary with initial-letter support.

questions.mappingNote: All seven printed parts assess recognition and interpretation of variation models; each maps to its own editable cloze response.
questions.methodNote: The question supplies the direct and inverse variation terminology, scaling statements and substitution method. No separate teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Select y=kx from direct variation, find k from the known pair, then substitute the new x; the requested sequence explicitly guides both steps.

questions.mappingNote: The known pair determines the direct variation constant and the new x determines y. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Use the substitution method stated in Fundamentals 1(e): form the direct variation model, determine k, then substitute the new input.

classification.difficultyReason: Select y=k/x, determine k from a known pair, then rearrange the calibrated model to find x from a new y.

questions.mappingNote: Fundamentals 1(c) and 1(e) on the source page support the model and substitution method; separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Use inverse variation and substitute the known pair to determine k, then solve the model for x.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the explicitly supplied inverse-square model to isolate k, evaluate y at a new x, and round the final result to three decimal places.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses calibration and evaluation of an inverse-power model. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Substitute into the explicitly supplied inverse-square model, solve for k and evaluate y without intermediate rounding.

classification.difficultyReason: Find two constants from the common initial values, then calculate the intermediate y before using the inverse model to find z; this requires routine linked procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Both relationships and all initial values are contained in this question. It assesses linked direct and inverse variation without depending on another question. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Calibrate each supplied model using the common set of values. Calculate the new y before using the inverse model to calculate z.

classification.difficultyReason: Calibrate the supplied square-root model, substitute the new period, then isolate and square the square root to recover the length.

questions.mappingNote: A non-unit power and solving for length are directly assessed. Length remains in centimetres throughout. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Use the supplied square-root model, determine k from the known period and length, then solve for the new length by isolating and squaring its square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the explicit inverse-square relationship into I=k/d², find the constant from one measurement, and directly evaluate at the new distance.

questions.mappingNote: The verbal inverse-square relationship supports the selected skill. The question supplies its own data and units; separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Translate inverse-square variation into a model, substitute the given measurements to determine k and evaluate at the requested distance.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the stated inverse-square relationship for the fixed masses, determine k from the given force and separation, and substitute the new separation.

questions.mappingNote: The inverse-square relationship and fixed masses directly support model-inverse-variation-power.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. The question explicitly requires forming an inverse-square model, substituting the known force and distance to determine k, then evaluating the model.

classification.difficultyReason: Form an inverse model from sales data, evaluate it at a new price, and connect its unbounded prediction near zero price to finite real demand.

questions.mappingNote: Calculating demand and evaluating the model's realism directly assess solve-variation-problems.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. The stated inverse relationship supports D=k/p, substitution to determine k, evaluation and a contextual explanation of the model's limitations.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate inverse-cube variation into a model, determine its constant, then rearrange and take a cube root to recover y.

questions.mappingNote: Forming x=k/y^3 and recovering the denominator variable directly assess model-inverse-variation-power.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. The question explicitly requires an inverse-cube model; determine k by substitution, rearrange for y cubed and take the cube root.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine inverse time–speed and direct speed–current relationships, calibrate and evaluate the resulting model, then assess its assumptions about swimmer speed and current direction.

questions.mappingNote: Problem 1 and its three printed parts form one shared swimmer-model task.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was unavailable. The question explicitly supplies direct and inverse variation relationships; combine them, determine the constant by substitution, then evaluate and assess the model.

classification.difficultyReason: Select drag coefficients and transfer a calibrated constant between shapes, then combine the supplied formulas to recognise that a 10% density reduction changes squared speed inversely and requires a square root.

questions.mappingNote: The model and five-column data table belong to the shared stem. The density explanation is permanent supplied information immediately before the part (b) task.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was unavailable. Use the supplied formula to determine the common constant, rearrange for area, and combine the two supplied formulas to compare terminal velocities.

classification.difficultyReason: Calibrate the supplied squared-period/cubed-distance model, retain the unrounded constant, recover a positive period and convert units, then interpret the physical assumptions limiting the model. The algebra is guided; identifying contextual limitations is the hardest demand.

questions.mappingNote: All three printed parts share the same Kepler model. The printed distances are retained pending resolution of their physical units.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was unavailable. Substitute into the supplied power-variation model, retain the exact constant for the second calculation, and take the positive square root for a period.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires splitting absolute-value equations into sign cases, solving linear and quadratic equations, and rejecting candidates using nonnegativity or substitution; part (g) combines these routine procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a)–(h) directly assess absolute value equations; (g) also requires factoring quadratics.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Independently solved using the two signs of an absolute value, the nonnegative right-hand-side condition and candidate verification.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses the nonnegative range of absolute value, then represents the same conclusion by sketching a translated V and a horizontal line with no intersections.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) tests the range of absolute value; (b) requires the same conclusion graphically.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Use nonnegativity and graph intersections, as explicitly required by the question.

classification.difficultyReason: Finds each vertex from the zero of the linear argument and uses intercepts, reflection and vertical scaling to sketch four familiar absolute-value graphs.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess transformed absolute value graphs.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Locate the zero of the argument and the y-intercept, then use the sign and coefficient to sketch each V.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise each reciprocal graph, select the correct quadrants from the sign of the constant, and substitute a convenient x-value to label one point.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess y=k/x sketches with one labelled point.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Substitute a convenient x-value, identify quadrants and sketch branches approaching the coordinate axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate inverse proportionality into y=k/x, determine k from the supplied pair, then reuse that constant to calculate a new value; the parts explicitly guide the sequence.

questions.mappingNote: Parts form one dependent inverse-proportion modelling task; all numerical givens are retained in the block.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Form y=k/x, calculate k=xy, then substitute the new x-value.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify constant worker-hours for a fixed job, solve for workers or time, and convert the fractional hour into minutes.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts share the complete 12-worker, 3-hour job stimulus and directly assess applied inverse proportion.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Model a fixed job using constant worker-hours, then solve for workers or time.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the square in one or both variables, read the centre and radius, then use coordinate extrema to sketch each circle.

questions.mappingNote: Both source equations directly assess circle centres, radii and coordinate sketches. This method has not been reconciled against the textbook's teaching examples.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The authored solution completes the square separately in x and y, then reads the centre and radius from the standard circle equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the centres and radii from Question 8 to find horizontal and vertical extrema and express them as closed intervals.

questions.mappingNote: Each unlettered response corresponds to one circle in Question 8. The answer book adds (a) and (b); the student question does not print separate part labels.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The solution uses centre coordinates plus or minus the radius to identify closed horizontal and vertical intervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the supplied graphs; in part (b), use the vertical chord midpoint to infer the centre, calculate the radius, then substitute axis conditions to find all intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) gives the centre through dashed coordinate guides and a y-axis tangency. Part (b) gives a vertical chord from y=0 to y=-6 and the centre's x-coordinate. These determine the keyed equations exactly.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The authored solutions use the centre-radius equation; part (b) uses the midpoint of the vertical chord and the distance to the origin.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate passing through the origin into a²+b²=8 for the centre, choose suitable coordinates and use sign variations to construct four distinct circle equations.

questions.mappingNote: The printed radius gives r squared equal to 8. The key's independent sign combinations satisfy the conditions, but the source gives no condition excluding the remaining centres with a squared plus b squared equal to 8.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The solution substitutes the origin into the general centre-radius equation to test the stated conditions.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest demand is independently exploring parameter choices and classifying graph families, connecting relative coefficient magnitudes and coincident or distinct argument zeros to corners, flat sections and cancellation. The later piecewise calculation and sketch are strongly scaffolded, but the initial investigation requires non-trivial generalisation across algebraic and graphical representations.

questions.mappingNote: Graphical investigation of absolute-value functions is the closest catalogue skill. The response explains possible sign-change locations without substituting an unrelated method.
questions.methodNote: The introduction recalls single absolute-value graphs. The assigned activity explicitly uses graphing software to investigate sums and differences; Question 2 supplies a sign-region scaffold.

existingTransferReview.note: Decision 2 (James, 11 November 2026): published on the recorded review covering each question's current content; no new model review.

bankProjection.note: Source-confirmed category headings are omitted only from bank prompts and presentation. Explicit equivalent fraction notation repairs satisfy bank validation. Source booklet content and all questions are retained.
